transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-11
Start: 10:00 PT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Arjun Patel (Redwood); Samira Lopez, Derek Wu, Nate Brooks, Ivy Ramos (Orchid Labs)
Links shared: https://redwood.company/benchmarks/orchid-2026-09 (benchmark sheet), SSO/SAML checklist (doc link)

Summary:
Quick check-in on POC economics: tokens per dollar, caching hit rates, batching tradeoffs. Agreed next steps to run a 24h steady-state benchmark on a dedicated pool and to test prefix cache tuning; plan for a short deep-dive next Wednesday if results deviate.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh we'll kick off quick, we have a tight agenda this morning — cost per unit, caching numbers from last week, and a couple of follow ups.
[00:15] Samira Lopez: cool thanks maya, i'll jump in, um we've been watching the tokens per dollar numbers on the sheet, so like, there was a big delta between the q4 run and the int8 experiment — wanted to get your read on that.
[00:30] Arjun Patel: yeah so short answer — quantization did reduce GPU utilization slightly but introduced a longer decode time per token in our obs for that model variant, so tokens/sec went down a bit, but cost per token still improved at the per-hour pricing we used. it's one of those tradeoffs.
[00:45] Derek Wu: are we comparing the same sequence length distribution? our real traffic skews longer than the synthetic tests in the sheet, so i'm concerned the numbers aren't apples-to-apples.
[01:00] Maya Chen: good call. on the sheet we had two distributions: synth-short (avg 64) and user-long (avg 256). the q4 run you saw was run on synth-short which explains some of the gap.
[01:12] Nate Brooks: okay that explains. can you run the q4 vs fp16 with the 256 distribution? that's the one that matches our prod.
[01:18] Arjun Patel: yes we can, that's exactly what the 24hr steady-state will test — steady qps, realistic SLs, and KV/prefix caching toggled to capture cache hit effects.
[01:26] [01:30] Ivy Ramos: quick question on prefix caching — in the last run our hit rate was only 12% which is lower than we'd expected given repeated prompts. is that because of dedupe mismatch or tokenization?
[01:40] Arjun Patel: likely both. our prefix cache is sensitive to tokenization differences and small semantic variations. we can enable fuzzy prefix matching and increase the cache window; that typically bumps hit rate 10-20 percentage points but with more memory and slightly higher lookup overhead.
[01:56] Samira Lopez: memory tradeoff is fine, we have slack on nodes, but we care about p95 latency — if caching lookup time adds and we lose p95 SLA that's an issue.
[02:08] Arjun Patel: right — for Orchid we recommended a two-tier cache: hot in-GPU KV for exact prefix hits (sub-ms), secondary in-host LRU for fuzzy matches (~5-10ms). that keeps p95 within bounds while recovering tokens.
[02:24] Derek Wu: can you share numbers? what's the expected tokens/$ improvement if hit rate goes from 12% to 35%?
[02:34] Maya Chen: on the benchmark sheet i put a quick calc: with our current workload and model (rw-13b-q4-like), each cached prefix saves ~120 tokens on average, at $0.00012 per token-equivalent hour metric, moving to 35% yields around 18-22% cost improvement overall. rough numbers.
[02:50] Samira Lopez: that's significant. how confident are you in the 120 tokens per hit figure?
[02:56] Arjun Patel: it's derived from sample traces (we used 5k requests). if you push us full prod traces the average saved tokens might shift — that's why we want the 24hr run on dedicated with your traces.
[03:10] [03:15] Maya Chen: side note — batching. we increased batch size from 8 to 24 in last week's run and throughput jumped but p95 increased from 180ms to 420ms.
[03:26] Nate Brooks: 420ms is borderline for our UI flows, can't go above 300.
[03:30] Arjun Patel: we can do dynamic batching policies — small batches for interactive routes (UI) and large batches for background tasks. Redwood routing supports per-route policies so you get the best of both worlds.
[03:42] Ivy Ramos: do you have CPU overhead numbers for batching? our nodes are CPU constrained.
[03:48] Arjun Patel: batching is GPU-bound largely, but the pre/post processing and I/O are CPU. we measured an extra 6-8% CPU at batch 24 versus batch 8. these are in the sheet under "batching_cpu_impacts".
[04:02] Derek Wu: alright, what's our immediate low-risk change to improve tokens/$ without touching latency SLA?
[04:08] Maya Chen: enable hot in-GPU prefix cache for exact matches, drop global batch from 24 to 12 for interactive routes, and enable token-level KV caching for repeated completions. Those are low-risk config flips.
[04:20] Samira Lopez: sounds good. any vendor lock or config we should worry about if we later move to dedicated vs hosted?
[04:27] Arjun Patel: configs are portable — same runtime and flags across hosted and dedicated; the only diffs are memory sizes and kernel choices which the runtime picks automatically. so moving to Dedicated is mostly infra provisioning.
[04:40] [04:45] Nate Brooks: security/regulatory question — our legal team wants to see audit log retention and KMS usage in dedicated, any updates?
[04:52] Maya Chen: yes, for VPC Dedicated we support customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and audit logs with configurable retention. i'll share the security pack (SOC2 summary, KMS guide, audit log schema).
[05:05] Samira Lopez: great, please include sample retention ranges, because we may need seven years for some records for compliance.
[05:13] Maya Chen: note taken.
[05:15] [05:20] Derek Wu: about cost math — the tokens/sec/$ metric you show, what's the denominator? is it tokens per dollar of GPU amortized cost only? or does it include infra overhead?
[05:30] Arjun Patel: good question. the sheet currently shows tokens per dollar of total instance-hour cost (GPU + host CPU + network egress estimate). we can also show a pure-GPU-only calc if you want.
[05:40] Samira Lopez: show both please. we have separate finance buckets.
[05:45] Maya Chen: will add a split column.
[05:47] [06:00] Arjun Patel: another nuance — cold KV warmups. first-hit penalties can exaggerate cost if you have many unique prefixes; we saw this on day-1 of the test where warmup tokens spiked. steady-state helps amortize that.
[06:14] Ivy Ramos: do you have an estimated break-even time for the cache warmup?
[06:18] Arjun Patel: for Orchid's request patterns i estimate 6-12 hours to reach steady hit rates if you have moderate repetition. we'll confirm with the 24h run.
[06:26] [06:30] Samira Lopez: ok we can do the 24hr. Derek will spin up the dedicated dev pool.
[06:36] Derek Wu: yes i'll provision a small 4-GPU dedicated pool, same region, add subnet and give Arjun access.
[06:40] Maya Chen: perfect. also we found batching+quantization combos behave differently per model family — e.g., 13b q4 had better tokens/$ at batch 12 than 24, but other models liked 24. so keep an open mind and run the matrix.
[06:56] Nate Brooks: can you give us a sample matrix you'd run?
[07:00] Arjun Patel: sure — we'll run: batch sizes [8,12,16,24], quant modes [fp16, q4, q8 if available], cache modes [off, hot-gpu-only, hot+fuzzy], and two seq distributions (avg 64, avg 256). total permutations ~48; we'll sample over 24 hours with steady QPS.
[07:18] Samira Lopez: that seems heavy but ok if it gives us reliable economics.
[07:22] Maya Chen: last week we also tested model fallback routing — cheaper model for non-critical routes — that saved about 9% cost when routed correctly. you might want to map routes that tolerate lower quality.
[07:35] Ivy Ramos: what about failures — if cheaper model fails, do you have automatic fallback?
[07:40] Arjun Patel: yes there's automated fallback policies and circuit breakers. we'll show a config example in the playbook.
[07:48] [07:55] Derek Wu: any surprises from the last run?
[08:00] Arjun Patel: one surprise: the tokenizer differences between our prep pipeline and the runtime caused 4% extra tokens in some prompts — small but compound over scale. we recommended normalizing tokenization at the platform edge.
[08:12] Samira Lopez: noted — we'll check our pipeline.
[08:15] Maya Chen: quick recap: Arjun runs the 24hr matrix on dedicated with the 256-length distribution; Derek will provide VPC creds and traces; Maya sends the playbook and updated sheet; Samira will circulate finance buckets.
[08:30] Nate Brooks: and we'll reconvene next Wednesday for a deep-dive if there are outliers, otherwise a short sync.
[08:35] Maya Chen: yes — i'll schedule a 60 minute deep dive Weds 9/16 10am PT.
[08:40] [08:45] Samira Lopez: one last thing — any rough ETA on the expected cost improvement if we get cache hit to 35% and batching tuned? number we can pitch internally?
[08:52] Arjun Patel: conservatively 20% improvement tokens/$; optimistically up to 30% if fallbacks and routing reduce load on the heavy model.
[08:59] Maya Chen: okay thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the sheet and action items.
[09:03] [09:10] Derek Wu: thanks all bye.
[09:12] End meeting.

Notes on transcription style: speaker labels include role sometimes, timestamps approximate. minor mishearings: "q4" sometimes transcribed "cue 4", "KV" as "K V", product names slightly off in some spots.
